title: Reconciliation through Christ and Faith
english: The Paul of the Law, made wise by the divine Spirit, guarantees that those who believe in the Son will escape the charge concerning the glory of the created gods.

Moreover, he also calls “atheists” those before this time who knew only God the Father apart from the Son — since their knowledge does not come to completion in works — writing here that: “Remember that at one time you, the Gentiles in the flesh — the so-called uncircumcision by the so-called circumcision made by hand in the flesh — that you were at that time apart from Christ, estranged from the hope of Israel and strangers to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and godless in the world.” (Eph 2:12).

And elsewhere: “But then, not knowing God, you were enslaved to those who by nature are not gods; but now, knowing God — or rather being known by God — how do you turn back again to the weak and poor elemental things, to which you want to be enslaved again anew?” (Gal 4:8-9).

But the saving proclamation concerning Christ and the Holy Spirit — ever new and never declining into old age — and the ecclesiastical order of the elder Law, he also deems more honorable, because it is perfect and has nothing unlawful troubling it, nor should anything better or greater be set forth in word or in manner; for in this matter he writes, saying that: “I was ‘in zeal persecuting the church; in righteousness under the law, blameless. But whatever were gains to me, these I have counted as loss for Christ. Indeed I also count all things as loss for the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things and count them as refuse, that I may gain Christ.’” (Phil 3:6-8).
And to the Romans: “For if the one coming preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive.”

Through that reconciliation — if one is reconciled to the Son, he is reconciled to God — the world was reconciled to God, and in Christ there is a covenant toward God for the world. For he has: 'just as God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and having established in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we plead on behalf of Christ as the God pleading through us. We pray on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.' (2 Cor 5:19).

And again, as if setting all other things aside, he preached, boasting loudly that even what seems reproachable for Christ is, through his philanthropy-driven economy, overflowing with all good repute and strength — doing this in practice — so that even the one who, from the glorious passion, does not look down upon the unbegotten, incorruptible, and unchangeable divinity might incur a charge of pride.

And he said such things: 'not that I have judged anything to be known among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.' (1 Cor 2:2). To the Romans: 'the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.' (Rom 3:22).

Through the faith spoken toward the Son, each is justified by God. To the Galatians: 'knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ, and we believed in Jesus Christ so that we might be justified from the faith of Christ and not from works of the law, because no flesh shall be justified by works of the law.' (Gal 2:16).
And he explains also to others that 'neither circumcision avails nor uncircumcision, but a new faith working through love.' (Gal 5:6). But as the word deepens the mind, it must be unfolded.

Therefore he intends to teach how the appearing of Christ found a new faith, the only one, for all men; according to which he left no place, neither in Judaism nor in Hellenism. And this could be understood also according to: 'behold, the old things have passed away, all things have become new.' (2 Cor 5:17).
